50443f339d38d5737a1f.text: Kirby did learn it the hard way. Sharing may be easy and rewarding but the consequences of sharing information that is unverified or worse, fake may affect other people in one way or another. So, what makes viewing different from listening? How different are these modalities?

27550928b05b8625c8f1.text: According to the Canadian Common Curriculum Framework, as cited by

6effac1e670a3b70634f.text: Donaghy, viewing is “an active process of attending and comprehending visual media such as television, advertising images, films, diagrams, symbols, photographs, videos, dramas, drawings, sculptures and paintings.

80111a46943764a26de2.text: Truth is the quality of being honest and not containing or telling any lie.

4c54c6d524520f196f89.text: Accuracy is the fact of being exact or correct.

d7f688824e893f2a4e56.text: How do you know that the information that you get from various resources

5f44888cdb29fd3f30ac.text: Most of the time we simply accept information relayed to us without actually

88699af2c6f32d7ec8db.text: evaluating the authenticity of the information. Understanding the truth can be viewed in many ways depending on the truth teller’s purpose. To carefully evaluate the truthfulness and accuracy of the material, you must be able to question the materials you find in various media platforms. You must be empowered with questions that will help you to seek clarity, question assumptions, and detect source reliability or bias.

a02074d7542851a694a4.text: One of the many ways to prevent ourselves from slipping into the pitfalls of

5925ba1cf16f88121a0c.text: deceptive viewing materials is to acquaint ourselves with deceptive techniques that people employ in different viewing materials.

93254c2920ad1dc5332b.text: The phrase “information disorder” was coined by Wardle (2017), First Draft

0d66dcc9b8fe3c30674e.text: inadequate to describe the complexity of deception. Furthermore, the term “fake news” has been weaponized, mostly by politicians and their supporters to attack the professional news media around the world. This lead Wardle (2017) to create the phrase information disorder.

dafc72c626b7826a7b5d.text: Information Disorder includes the following forms: Satire/ Parody Misleading

c442f68c81444da6ffb9.text: Content, Imposter Content, Fabricated Content, False Connection, False Context, and Manipulated content.

d4f7629f20877a81af51.text: According to Wardle, (2017) there are seven common forms of information disorder.

c6d784f31424b4c5ef75.text: 1.Satire/ Parody- These types of viewable texts have no intention to cause harm but

b35055c22ad6f71e20ba.text: has potential to fool. Content purporting to be satire will evade the fact-checkers, and frequently over time, the original context gets lost: people share and re-share not realizing the content is satire and believing that it is true.

517bb3b84f37e4712918.text: 2. Misleading Content- There are also texts that use misleading information to

cb8951c13e57a4c8437d.text: frame an issue or an individual. Some common examples of this technique are selection of a partial segment from a quote, creating statistics that support a particular claim but don’t take into account how the data set was created, or cropping a photo to frame an event in a particular way.

accf6dfef6cb761c351b.text: 3. Imposter Content- This is when genuine sources are impersonated. An example

c78c21af903cec41bd36.text: of this is when the logo of a well-known brand or name is used alongside false content. The goal of this deception is to increase the chance that people will trust the content without checking the content.

bd8afcdf0a811850f871.text: 4. Fabricated Content- The new content is 100% false. These texts are designed to

a8816242f195a6fb5555.text: deceive and to harm. New fake social media accounts are created to spread new and invented content from it.

d3554bcf7a2fb0c429a5.text: 5. False Connection- This is when headlines, visuals, or captions don’t support the

e3a2f71d603e6d9ce7cd.text: content. This technique makes claims about content via a sensational headline, only to find the headline is horribly disconnected from the actual article or piece of content.

9b0a6d8d38192bba69d8.text: 6. False Context- This is when genuine content is shared with false contextual

3aafc91ca264fcf63d3b.text: information. It often happens during a breaking news event when old imagery is re-shared, but it also happens when old news articles are re-shared as new, when the headline still potentially fits with contemporary events.

f858a5d8cbdb09a2def0.text: 7. Manipulated Content- This is when genuine information or imagery is

41704531fa88136b46f4.text: manipulated to deceive. The genuine content is tampered with or doctored in some way.

b9dd618384e87341912a.text: SOAPSTone method stands for (Speaker, Occasion, Audience, Purpose,

3538a18697d4f96c65e3.text: Subject and Tone). It is a method which can be used to determine the truthfulness and accuracy of the material viewed.

e8fc36815266ad98e494.text: It is a method for evaluating credibility of persuasive essays in conventional

f7bc99af9090a02fa9a8.text: print and media sources. This method is useful for English language learners and can be used for video clips, cartoons, news sources, speeches, software products, and websites. It deepens student’s thinking about technological sources and of information and allows practice in questioning authenticity. (Gregory & Burkman, 2012)

1cb314c103da631b2ba3.text: To evaluate the authenticity of materials viewed, the SOAPSTone is used as

10688a8761d0a3349c62.text: shown below. The table is divided into 3 (three) columns. Under the first column are the six (6) components of the method. Under the second column are the corresponding descriptions of each component. And under the last column are the critical questions which will help determine the truthfulness and accuracy of the material.

Element of Source Verification
Description/meaning
Critical Questions
Speaker
The voice communicating/speaking to the audience Example: Author
1. Is the author in the viewed material speaking for himself or using the voice or opinion of a particular person or group?
Occasion
Time or place; context that prompted the author or speaker to create the material Example: Election period, pandemic crisis
1. What has triggered the author’s material (presentation, website, or document)? 2. Are the reasons for creating the material based on events, emotions, data, or economics?
Audience
Group to which the material is intended Example: Consumers, employees, students
1. Toward whom is the material (presentation, website, or document) intended?
Purpose
The reason to of the author in creating the material Example: To give information To mislead the readers

1. What does the author want the intended audience to think or do as a result of reading or viewing the material? 2. What does the author want the unintended audience to think or do as a result of reading or viewing the material?
